results.title: Reconstructing Householder Vectors from Tall-Skinny QR (Ballard, Demmel, Grigori, Hoemmen, Knight — UCB/EECS-2013-175 Tech Report, full PDF)
results.snippet: This is the canonical full-text source for requirement #1 (the exact ORHR_COL / xUNHR_COL recurrence). Key recurrence stated explicitly: the Householder vectors representing an orthonormal Q can be recovered via an UNPIVOTED LU decomposition of (S - Q), where S is a diagonal sign matrix — i.e. Q = householder-reconstruct(LU(S - Q1)). This makes reconstruction GEMM/LU-heavy and parallel rather than a serial reflector chain, and recovers the flat (H,tau) for ~the same cost as TSQR itself. Directly enables emitting LAPACK-geqrf-compatible flat (H,tau) from an implicit TSQR Q — exactly the output contract (Q=householder_product(tril(H,-1),tau)). The tech-report version contains the full derivation and proofs omitted from the conference paper.

results.title: Reconstructing Householder vectors from Tall-Skinny QR — Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing (2015 journal version, Ballard et al.)
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed 2015 journal version (the citable 'Ballard-Demmel-Grigori-Hoemmen-Knight 2015' the question names). Shows how to combine TSQR efficiency in PANEL factorization with Householder-QR efficiency in TRAILING-matrix update inside a 2D blocked QR — precisely the architecture needed: TSQR tree for the grid-starved panel critical path, then reconstruct flat (H,tau) so the trailing update stays a standard compact-WY tensor-core GEMM. Addresses the bottleneck framing (panel = 45% critical path) head-on. OSTI open-access mirrors of this exist at osti.gov/servlets/purl/1236219 and /1315576 for the full text.

results.title: Communication-Avoiding QR Decomposition for GPUs (Anderson, Ballard, Demmel, Keutzer — IPDPS 2011, IEEE Xplore)
results.snippet: The foundational single-GPU CAQR/TSQR implementation paper for requirement #2. Runs the entire TSQR reduction-tree panel factorization on one GPU with compute-bound (not bandwidth-bound) kernels, mapping row-block leaves to thread blocks and merging R-factors up a binary tree WITHOUT device-wide O(n) barriers — exactly the mechanism to fill idle SMs at grid-starved batch=60/n=1024. Reports outperforming then-current GPU QR (MAGMA/CULA) for tall-skinny shapes because performance is independent of panel width. Free full text mirrored at academia.edu/16378463 and researchgate.net/publication/224257718.

results.title: Implementation of QR factorization of tall and very skinny matrices on current GPUs (2026 arXiv)
results.snippet: Most recent (2026) source matching the 'recent GPU technique' ask in requirements #3/#4. Targets TSQR specifically on CURRENT GPU hardware (relevant to B200/sm_100 tensor-core era), addressing how to map the tree reduction and per-leaf QR efficiently when the matrix is tall-and-very-skinny — i.e. the n x IB panel shape that is the critical path. Useful for concrete kernel-mapping and batching choices on modern architectures rather than the 2011-era hardware of the foundational papers.

results.title: Scalable QR Factorisation of Ill-Conditioned Tall-and-Skinny Matrices on Distributed GPU Systems (Mathematics 2025)
results.snippet: Directly addresses requirement #5's robustness constraint: ILL-CONDITIONED tall-and-skinny QR on GPUs, where naive CholeskyQR squares the condition number and fails (exactly the failure mode the checker's ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs probe). Covers re-orthogonalization / shifted-CholeskyQR2-style schemes that keep accuracy on bad-conditioned inputs while still using tensor-core-friendly GEMM building blocks. Bridges the speed-vs-numerical-robustness tradeoff the ranked-approaches list (req #6) must respect.

results.title: Advancing the distributed Multi-GPU ChASE library through algorithm optimization and NCCL (2023 arXiv)
results.snippet: 2023 GPU eigensolver work that uses TSQR-style communication-avoiding orthogonalization as a building block on multi-GPU; relevant to requirement #4 (recent 2023-2026 batched/GPU panel-orthogonalization practice) and shows a production-grade choice of TSQR vs CholeskyQR-with-reorthogonalization on tensor-core GPUs. Lower direct relevance because it is multi-GPU/distributed and eigensolver-oriented rather than single-device batched geqrf, but useful for the engineering tradeoffs of mapping the reduction tree to real hardware.

results.title: Reconstructing Householder Vectors from Tall-Skinny QR (Ballard, Demmel, Grigori, Hoemmen, Knight, Solomonik) — UC Berkeley EECS-2013-175 full PDF
results.snippet: THE primary source the question asks for, and the full-text PDF (the most directly usable form). This is the canonical Ballard-Demmel-Grigori-Hoemmen-Knight tech report giving the exact reconstruction recurrences: do TSQR to get the implicit Q and R, then reconstruct the FLAT Householder (V, tau / T) representation with the SAME asymptotic communication cost and only a small extra computational cost. The key identity is the one ORHR_COL formalizes: if Q_in is the thin orthonormal factor, you recover Householder vectors V and block-reflector T such that Q_in = Q_out*S with S a sign diagonal. This directly addresses bottleneck items (1) and (2): how to combine a tree-reduction TSQR panel (filling idle SMs at grid-starved batch) with cheap, GEMM-heavy reconstruction that emits geqrf-compatible (H, tau). Contains the per-leaf/merge recurrences and the apply-to-trailing-matrix analysis.

results.title: Reconstructing Householder vectors from Tall-Skinny QR — Inria HAL (Grigori et al., journal version landing page)
results.snippet: Inria/HAL record for the published journal version (JPDC 2015), Grigori being a primary author. Confirms the central claim load-bearing for the panel-bottleneck strategy: TSQR is more communication-efficient than serial Householder QR but produces a DIFFERENT Q representation that is costly to apply to the trailing matrix; the paper's contribution is reconstructing the standard Householder representation 'with the same asymptotic communication efficiency and little extra computational cost,' yielding parallel QR with significantly lower latency than Householder QR and lower bandwidth/latency than CAQR. Directly motivates replacing the serial reflector chain (~45% of runtime) with a tree reduction plus reconstruction. Good stable citation/abstract; pairs with the Berkeley PDF for the equations.

results.title: LAPACK: dorhr_col / unhr_col — reference documentation for the Householder reconstruction routine
results.snippet: THE exact LAPACK routine named in the question (xORHR_COL / xUNHR_COL), with its precise output contract — which maps almost 1:1 onto the checker's required FLAT (H, tau). Documents that ORHR_COL takes an M-by-N matrix Q_in with orthonormal columns and reconstructs Householder vectors V(i) representing Q_out with Q_in = Q_out*S (S an N-by-N diagonal of +/-1); V is stored in A and T is returned in the SAME format as GEQRT, so the result is directly geqrf-compatible. Crucially gives the block-reflector WY form Q_out(i)=I - V_B(i) T_B(i) V_B(i)^T (tensor-core-GEMM-friendly reconstruction) and the sign-correction R_out = S*R_in. This is the blueprint for emitting flat (H, tau) from any orthonormal Q_in (TSQR or CholeskyQR), addressing items (1) and (2). Authoritative API reference; see the .f source for the literal recurrence.

results.title: LAPACK SORHR_COL Fortran source — literal reconstruction algorithm/recurrence
results.snippet: The actual SORHR_COL Fortran source: the literal, copyable algorithm for Householder reconstruction (the recurrence the question explicitly asks for at 'code-level specificity'). Shows exactly how V, T (block reflector, GEQRT format), and the sign diagonal D=S are computed from an orthonormal Q_in, including the diagonal-sign bookkeeping and the column-blocked T construction. This is what you port to Triton/CuTe to make the reconstruction step GEMM-heavy and parallel rather than O(batch*n^3) serial. Pairs with the dorhr_col API doc; together they answer item (1) — making reconstruction cheap and tensor-core-friendly.

results.title: QR factorization of ill-conditioned tall-and-skinny matrices on distributed-memory systems (2024)
results.snippet: Recent (2024) work tying together the three threads most relevant to the panel bottleneck AND the numerical-robustness constraint: CholeskyQR-family panel factorization, Householder reconstruction (ORHR_COL-style), and ILL-CONDITIONED inputs. The checker's test set includes ill-conditioned/rank-deficient/near-collinear matrices where naive CholeskyQR (which squares the condition number) FAILS — this paper addresses exactly that regime via shifted/randomized/multi-pass CholeskyQR plus reconstruction to recover a robust orthonormal factor that you can then feed to ORHR_COL to emit flat (H, tau). Directly informs item (5) (mixed-precision/robust panel) and the novel-combination ask in item (6): TSQR-or-shiftedCholeskyQR panel -> reconstruct Householder -> GEMM trailing update. Recent enough to reflect modern GPU/tensor-core practice.

results.title: CholeskyQR with Randomization and Pivoting for Tall Matrices (CQRRPT) (2023)
results.snippet: 2023 paper on a single-pass CholeskyQR variant (randomization + pivoting, CQRRPT) that achieves Householder-level numerical stability for tall matrices at much lower cost than communication-avoiding Householder QR. Relevant as a robust, GEMM-heavy alternative panel factorization whose orthonormal output Q can be post-processed by ORHR_COL into flat (H, tau): it offers a way to break the serial reflector dependency chain (the ~45% critical path) using randomized preconditioning + Cholesky (cheap, tensor-core-friendly) while still passing the ill-conditioned/near-rank-deficient checker cases that plain CholeskyQR fails. Feeds items (5) and (6) (the robust mixed-precision panel and the novel buildable combinations); pairs naturally with the 2024 ill-conditioned-TSQR paper above. Note: the pivoting changes column order, so to emit a non-pivoted flat (H, tau) you must account for / undo the permutation.

results.title: Shifted CholeskyQR for Computing the QR Factorization of Ill-Conditioned Matrices (Fukaya, Kannan, Nakatsukasa, Yamamoto, Yanagisawa; SISC 2020)
results.snippet: THE canonical robust-CholeskyQR reference and directly the bottleneck-relevant paper. Gives the exact shift formula sigma = 11*(m*n + n*(n+1))*u*||A||_2 (or the practical sqrt(m)*u*||A||_F^2 form), proving the shifted Gram matrix A^T A + sigma*I stays positive-definite so Cholesky succeeds even at cond ~ u^{-1}. The key for the panel: shifted-CholeskyQR3 = sCQR (preconditioner) + CholeskyQR2, all BLAS-3 GEMM + small-Cholesky, NO extended precision needed, NO serial reflector chain. This is the natural way to make the n x IB panel tensor-core-GEMM-heavy and parallel across the grid-starved batch=60/n=1024 regime, IF you then reconstruct flat (H,tau) via ORHR_COL from the resulting Q,R. Numerical robustness matches the contest's ill-conditioned/clustered-SV test set.

results.title: Randomized LU-Householder CholeskyQR (rLHC: SLHC3 / SSLHC3) (2024)
results.snippet: Newest (2024) and the most aggressive robust-panel idea: use an LU factor of A (or of its sketch) as the preconditioner instead of a shift, because L is far better conditioned than A itself, then finish with Cholesky/Householder. SLHC3 = single-sketch, SSLHC3 = multi-sketch. Handles arbitrary condition number with provable orthogonality ~ unit roundoff. Most relevant novel-combination seed: replace the serial Householder panel with sketch->LU-precondition->CholeskyQR (all GEMM/TRSM, parallel-friendly), then emit flat (H,tau) by ORHR_COL on the well-conditioned result. Directly attacks the 45% panel critical path with tensor-core-amenable work.

results.title: Analysis of Randomized Householder-Cholesky QR Factorization with Multisketching (rand_cholQR) (Higgins, Szyld, Boman, Yamazaki; Numer. Math. 2025)
results.snippet: Proves rand_cholQR with one or two sketches is as STABLE as shifted-CholeskyQR3 for any numerically full-rank matrix, with orthogonality error O(u). Critically includes a REAL GPU implementation (Kokkos Kernels -> cuBLAS) on A100 showing it is as fast as or faster than CholeskyQR2 for tall-skinny matrices — i.e. a robust panel built almost entirely from tensor-core GEMM, exactly the property needed to fill idle SMs in the grid-starved batch=2/n=4096 and batch=60/n=1024 cases. Sketch is 2n x m (sparse-sign), B = A R1^{-1} preconditions before CholeskyQR so the condition-squaring is avoided. Pairs with ORHR_COL to produce the contest's flat (H,tau).

results.title: Mixed-Precision Cholesky QR Factorization and Its Case Studies on Multicore CPU with Multiple GPUs (Yamazaki, Tomov, Dongarra; SISC 2015)
results.snippet: The foundational mixed-precision-CholeskyQR paper and the direct template for the contest's precision angle: keep A and Q in working (FP32) precision but accumulate the Gram matrix A^T A in DOUBLED precision, which turns the orthogonality error's quadratic cond-dependence into LINEAR. This is exactly the tf32x3 / 3xTF32 error-corrected accumulation trick applied to the PANEL Gram, not the trailing GEMM — letting a CholeskyQR-style panel stay FP32-flat-(H,tau) accurate on ill-conditioned inputs. Shows the multi-GPU communication-avoiding structure (one global reduction) that maps to the one-CTA-per-row-block GPU tree.

results.title: Scalable QR Factorisation of Ill-Conditioned Tall-and-Skinny Matrices on Distributed GPU Systems (2025); arXiv:2405.04237
results.snippet: 2025 GPU-focused treatment of the full robust-TSQR stack with concrete thresholds and a panel-blocked reorthogonalization scheme (mCQR2GS) that interleaves CholeskyQR steps with Gram-Schmidt reorthogonalization per panel of adjustable width b (e.g. b~300 for cond 1e15). Gives the switching thresholds (CQR < 1e8, sCQR3 up to 1e15), the shift sigma = sqrt(m)*u*||A||_F^2, and notes Tensor-Core GEMMs in QR are tall-skinny hence suboptimal — useful caution for the panel. Relevant as the recipe for choosing per-shape robustness level (cheap path for well-conditioned batch=640/n=512, expensive reorth only when a cheap condition estimate flags ill-conditioning).

results.title: CholeskyQR with Randomization and Pivoting for Tall Matrices (CQRRPT) (Melnichenko, Balabanov, Murray, Demmel, Mahoney, Luszczek; SIMAX 2024)
results.snippet: Adds column PIVOTING to randomized CholeskyQR, which is the missing piece for the contest's RANK-DEFICIENT and near-rank-deficient inputs (plain CholeskyQR2/shifted assume full column rank and can fail rank-deficient cases). Sketch-and-pivot reveals numerical rank cheaply, then a single Cholesky on the well-conditioned pivoted preconditioned matrix gives stable Q,R. Relevant as the robustness backstop so a fast randomized/shifted panel still passes the rank-deficient/near-collinear test matrices before reconstructing flat (H,tau) via ORHR_COL.

results.title: High Performance Householder QR Factorization on Emerging GPU Architectures Using Tensor Cores (IEEE TPDS 2024)
results.snippet: Most on-target recent (2024) source: uses RECURSIVE QR panel + compact-WY/UT-transform specifically to convert the tall-skinny panel GEMMs into square tensor-core GEMMs (the panel's inner GEMMs are otherwise memory-bound and run poorly on tensor cores). Directly addresses the question's core thesis -- that after the trailing update is at roofline, the panel is the bottleneck -- and shows recursion as the lever to GEMM-ify it. Closest published work to the proposed novel combinations for B200. (Paywalled HTML/abstract; full text via authors' preprint.)

results.title: LAPACK: dgeqrt3 — recursive QR factorization with the T factor (compact WY)
results.snippet: The exact routine the question names. geqrt3 recursively computes QR with compact-WY: Q = I - V T V^T, splitting the n columns vertically ~in half down a binary tree of ceil(log2(n/b)) levels until columns < threshold, replacing the serial reflector-by-reflector chain with BLAS-3 recursion. Gives the precise recurrence (recurse left block, apply to right block, recurse right, merge T via the off-diagonal T12 = -T11 (V1^T V2) T22 update) needed to shorten the panel critical path while still emitting a single flat (V, T) -> recoverable (H, tau). Implements Elmroth-Gustavson (IBM J. Res. Develop. 44(4), 2000).

results.title: Elmroth & Gustavson — Applying recursion to serial and parallel QR factorization leads to better performance
results.snippet: Origin paper for geqrt3's recursive compact-WY panel. Key data point for the panel-bottleneck argument: the recursive panel makes the factorization a BLAS-3 (level-3) operation, giving ~20% over LAPACK DGEQRF on large square matrices and up to ~3x on TALL-THIN matrices -- precisely the n x IB panel shape that dominates the critical path here. Documents the hybrid scheme (divide into column panels, recurse within each panel) needed because pure recursion's flops grow cubically in n; gives merge recurrences for the T factor. Foundational for any recursive-panel approach on the batch=60/n=1024 grid-starved regime.

results.title: Batch QR Factorization on GPUs: Design, Optimization, and Tuning (ICCS 2022, Abdelfattah/Tomov/Dongarra)
results.snippet: Directly on the BATCHED-QR sub-question. MAGMA batched geqrf design: relies on batch level-3 BLAS for the trailing update (strong on square, GPU-saturating batch=640/n=512 regime) but notes applying block Householder reflectors efficiently on GPU often requires re-organizing steps into kernels that do NOT follow the LAPACK structure -- the exact freedom the (H,tau) output contract permits. Covers tuning of panel width / kernel design across batched matrix sizes; the design-and-tuning reference for the GPU-saturating vs GPU-starved regime split.

results.title: Programming Parallel Dense Matrix Factorizations with Look-Ahead and OpenMP
results.snippet: The look-ahead angle (panel-critical-path shortening that is NOT communication-avoiding). Static look-ahead embedded directly in the factorization code overlaps the serial panel factorization of step k+1 with the highly-parallel trailing update of step k, hiding the panel off the critical path. Gives the concrete dependency-restructuring scheme. Caveat for this workload (also flagged by the MAGMA papers): look-ahead stops helping when the trailing update is too small to overlap -- i.e. exactly the grid-starved batch=2/n=4096 and batch=60/n=1024 cases -- so it must be paired with recursion/TSQR there. Useful precisely because it bounds where look-ahead alone wins.

results.title: MAGMA: Enabling exascale performance with accelerated BLAS and LAPACK for diverse GPU architectures (2024)
results.snippet: 2024 MAGMA reference for the GPU panel/trailing strategy and its limits. Confirms the hybrid look-ahead overlaps CPU panel factorization with GPU trailing update, but is explicitly 'not efficient for small sizes, since the updates are no longer compute intensive' and fail to overlap panel + transfer -- the precise failure mode of the dominant small/grid-starved shapes here, motivating an on-GPU recursive or tree-based panel instead of CPU-hybrid look-ahead. Establishes the modern baseline the question must beat and why the standard look-ahead recipe does not transfer to these batched regimes.

results.title: High Performance Householder QR Factorization on Emerging GPU Architectures Using Tensor Cores (Leng, Zou, Wang, Wu, Zhang — IEEE TPDS 36(3):422-436, Mar 2025)
results.snippet: The single most on-target paper. Directly attacks the original question's exact bottleneck: the inner QR GEMMs are tall-and-skinny and memory-bound on tensor cores. Its core technique is RECURSIVE QR factorization (geqrt3-style divide-and-conquer panel) to convert tall-skinny GEMMs into square/large GEMMs that hit tensor-core roofline — this is precisely the 'panel critical-path shortening that is NOT communication-avoiding' the user asked for (item 3). Covers mixed precision: extends FP16-tensor-core QR to FP32 (via FP16 tensor cores, i.e. error-corrected / split emulation analogous to 3xTF32) and FP64 (via INT8 cores), and explicitly switches Gram-Schmidt -> Householder to fix orthogonality loss on ill-conditioned inputs (item 5). Maps to the trailing-update GEMM-ification plus the recursive panel. ACM mirror DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2024.3522776 is paywalled; IEEE Xplore is the canonical landing page.

results.title: Batch QR Factorization on GPUs: Design, Optimization, and Tuning (Boukaram/Abdelfattah et al., ICCS 2022 — MAGMA batched geqrf)
results.snippet: The canonical MAGMA batched-geqrf design paper and the direct answer to item 4 (batched QR, GPU-saturating vs GPU-starved regimes). Documents the THREE-strategy switch by matrix size: (a) fully-fused single-kernel factorization for n<=32, (b) fused panel+update kernels for medium sizes, (c) classical LAPACK-style blocked panel + batch-GEMM trailing for large sizes — exactly the regime-dependent dispatch the user needs for batch=640/n=512 (saturating) vs batch=2/n=4096 (starved). Reports MAGMA up to 2.3x/3.3x (s/d) over KBLAS and 16-25x over cuBLAS via aggressive batch-GEMM use. Sections explicitly cover panel optimization (5.5), trailing update (6), and sub-warp tuning (7). Mirror also at iccs-meeting.org/archive/iccs2022/papers/133500064.pdf.

results.title: Implementation of QR factorization of tall and very skinny matrices on current GPUs (Jonas Thies & Melven Röhrig-Zöllner, 2026)
results.snippet: Newest result (2026, H100-targeted) and squarely on the panel/TSQR critical path that is now ~45% of the user's runtime. Tall-and-VERY-skinny is exactly the n x IB panel shape and the grid-starved regime (batch=60/n=1024). Includes H100 roofline models and benchmarks vs library baselines (filenames confirm cuSOLVER/MAGMA-style comparisons). Most directly informs how to keep the tall-skinny panel reduction bandwidth-bound-optimal and fill idle SMs — the core of items 2 and 6. Worth fetching the full text from arxiv.org/abs/2603.20889 for the per-leaf/merge recurrences.

results.title: Communication-Avoiding QR Decomposition for GPUs (Anderson, Ballard, Demmel, Keutzer — LAWN 240 / UCB-EECS)
results.snippet: The canonical CAQR/TSQR-on-GPU reference, directly answering item 2 (row-block reduction tree replacing the serial reflector chain with O(log P) tree-reduction to fill idle SMs at grid-starved batch). Demmel is also a co-author of the Ballard-Demmel-Grigori-Hoemmen-Knight 'reconstructing Householder vectors from TSQR' work the user cites in item 1, so this is the upstream primitive for combining TSQR (implicit Q) with ORHR_COL to emit flat geqrf-compatible (H,tau). Describes mapping one-CTA-per-row-block and avoiding device-wide barriers. Reports speedups over MAGMA. Foundational for any TSQR-based panel design.

results.title: Batched QR and SVD Algorithms on GPUs with Applications in Hierarchical Matrix Compression (Boukaram, Turkiyyah, Keyes — Parallel Computing 2018 / KBLAS)
results.snippet: The KBLAS-batched-QR paper and the chief competitor MAGMA benchmarks against. Relevant to item 4: targets exactly the batch-of-small/medium-matrices regime (the batch=640/n=512 case) and the data-reuse-via-shared-memory strategy that caches the whole panel in fast memory for few-row matrices — the alternative to GEMM-ification when the matrix is small enough to fit on-chip. Useful as the design contrast to MAGMA's batch-GEMM approach for choosing the per-regime panel kernel.

results.title: High Accuracy Low Precision QR Factorization and Least Square Solver on GPU with TensorCore (Zhang, Baboulin et al., 2019)
results.snippet: Directly relevant to item 5 (mixed-precision robust QR on tensor cores). Establishes the FP16/TF32-tensor-core QR baseline plus iterative-refinement / re-orthogonalization to recover FP32-level accuracy and orthogonality on ill-conditioned inputs — the accuracy-recovery scheme needed to keep flat-(H,tau) valid against the checker's 20*n*eps32 / 100*n*eps32 bounds when forming reflectors in reduced precision. The precursor that the 2025 TPDS tensor-core paper builds on; ar5iv HTML version is readable at ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1912.05508.

claims.claim: Householder-based TSQR with a two-stage tree reduction (k thread blocks each factor m/k rows in shared memory, then a second stage reduces) reaches ~100% of roofline only for very few columns (n<=8) and degrades to ~6 TFlop/s by n=32 due to synchronization, instruction latency, and shared-memory transfers — practical only up to n<=64 columns on H100. This bounds the column count where this paper's tree-TSQR helps, well below the n=512-4096 panel/square regime in the research question.
claims.quote: Achieves "100% Roofline performance for very few columns (n<=8)" but requires careful shared-memory management, limiting practical use to n<=64 columns on H100 GPUs. ... "synchronization effects, instruction latencies and shared memory transfers limit the performance to roughly 6 TFlop/s (n=32)"

claims.claim: CholeskyQR-family methods (CholQR2, SVQB2) are conditionally stable: single-pass requires kappa_2(X) < sqrt(eps_mach), and even the two-pass variants only relax this to kappa_2(X) < eps_mach^{-0.5}. This confirms the research question's warning that CholeskyQR squares the condition number and fails ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs unless guarded by a second pass (and still bounded condition).
claims.quote: CholQR2 and SVQB2 require kappa_2(X) < sqrt(eps_mach) for single-pass stability. Two-pass variants (CholQR2, SVQB2) relax this to kappa_2(X) < eps_mach^{-0.5}.

claims.claim: The paper deliberately targets Q-less QR (returns neither Q nor its generating coefficients) to cut memory traffic, gaining a 3x (n=8) to 1.3x (n=32) speedup over SVQB2. This is a non-starter for the research question's output contract, which requires emitting the flat Householder factors (H, tau) so that householder_product reconstructs Q — so this paper's headline optimization is inapplicable.
claims.quote: The paper focuses on algorithms that "do not return Q or its generating coefficients at all" to reduce memory transfers. This optimization yields "a speed-up of 3 (for n=8 columns) to 1.3 (n=32)" compared to SVQB2.

claims.claim: These tall-skinny algorithms are explicitly memory-traffic-bound, not compute-bound, in the relevant column range: TSQR arithmetic intensity is only n/4 flops/byte and 'memory traffic dominates the computing time' for n<=32. By contrast, the research question's batched square panel (n=512+) is compute/latency-bound on the serial reflector chain, so the optimization levers differ (this paper offers no tensor-core / TF32 path — it omits tensor cores entirely).
claims.quote: The paper demonstrates that "memory traffic dominates the computing time" for n<=32 columns. ... No tensor-core exploitation (cuBLAS could improve n>=32 cases)

claims.claim: The reported tree-TSQR and SVQB2 implementations beat cuSOLVER by at least 10x for n=32 and >300x for n=8, showing that for narrow panels a custom shared-memory tree reduction massively outperforms the vendor library. This supports the research question's premise that custom kernels can beat library QR, but only in the very-skinny regime measured here.
claims.quote: **Speed-up vs. cuSOLVER:** "at least 10x for n=32" and ">>300 for n=8"

claims.claim: SORHR_COL performs Householder Reconstruction: given an M-by-N matrix Q_in with orthonormal columns (e.g. the implicit Q from a Cholesky-QR/TSQR), it reconstructs flat Householder vectors V(i) representing Q_out such that Q_in = Q_out*S, where S is an N-by-N diagonal sign matrix (+1/-1). This is exactly the step that converts a TSQR/CholeskyQR implicit-Q into a LAPACK geqrf-compatible flat (V, T) representation.
claims.quote: SORHR_COL takes an M-by-N real matrix Q_in with orthonormal columns as input, stored in A, and performs Householder Reconstruction (HR), i.e. reconstructs Householder vectors V(i) implicitly representing another M-by-N matrix Q_out, with the property that Q_in = Q_out*S, where S is an N-by-N diagonal matrix with diagonal entries equal to +1 or -1.

claims.claim: The reconstruction is driven by a modified (non-pivoted) LU/Gaussian-elimination factorization of (Q_in - [S;0]) = V*U: it calls SLAORHR_COL_GETRFNP to compute the LU factors V1 (unit lower-trapezoidal Householder vectors) and U (upper-triangular), simultaneously producing the sign vector D. This means the dominant work of HR is an LU factorization plus triangular solves, not a fresh QR — and the LU/TRSM kernels are GEMM-shaped and batchable.
claims.quote: Q_in - ( S ) = V * U

claims.claim: The diagonal sign matrix D is determined elementwise as D(i) = -SIGN(Q_in_i(i,i)) where Q_in_i is Q_in after i-1 steps of modified Gaussian elimination — i.e. the sign is read directly off the running LU pivot diagonal, so the sign step is O(N) bookkeeping interleaved with the LU, not an extra pass.
claims.quote: D(i) = -SIGN(Q_in_i(i,i)), where 1 <= i <= min(M,N), and Q_in_i is Q_in after performing i-1 steps of 'modified' Gaussian elimination.

claims.claim: The reconstructed reflectors compose as a single global product of block reflectors Q_out = Q_out(1)*Q_out(2)*...*Q_out(NOCB), each block being I - VB(i)*TB(i)*VB(i)^T in compact-WY form — so the output is a globally-composing flat Householder sequence (satisfying the contract that per-block reflectors must compose as one global householder_product), and the T factors are obtained via TRSM solving T(JB)*V1(JB)^T = (-1)*U(JB)*S(JB).
claims.quote: Q_out = Q_out(1) * Q_out(2) * ... * Q_out(NOCB), where each matrix Q_out(i) is given by: Q_out(i) = I - VB(i) * TB(i) * (VB(i))**T

claims.claim: If Q_in came from a QR factorization B = Q_in*R_in, then the reconstructed factors satisfy B = Q_out*(S*R_in) = Q_out*R_out, so R is recovered simply by sign-flipping rows of the original R_in by S — the R update after reconstruction is an O(N^2) per-matrix diagonal scaling, cheap relative to the panel.
claims.quote: If Q_in is the result of doing a QR factorization B = Q_in * R_in, then: B = Q_out * (S * R_in) = Q_out * R_out.

claims.claim: Randomized LU-Householder CholeskyQR (rLHC; variants SLHC3 single-sketch and SSLHC3 multi-sketch) achieves orthogonality error linear (not quadratic) in the problem size and removes the input condition-number requirement that breaks naive CholeskyQR2/SCholeskyQR3 on ill-conditioned matrices — directly addressing the research question's constraint that naive CholeskyQR squaring the condition number FAILS the ill-conditioned cases.
claims.quote: they do not require a condition of κ₂(X) for the input matrix X, which ensures the applicability of the algorithms ... ‖Q^⊤Q − I‖_F ≤ 6(mn𝐮 + n(n+1)𝐮)

claims.claim: The robustness mechanism is to replace the breakdown-prone Cholesky/LU-of-L step with an embedded HouseholderQR on the (sketched) L factor: when the L factor from LU is ill-conditioned, HouseholderQR is used to generate the upper-triangular factor instead of Cholesky, preventing numerical breakdown — a concrete recipe for a robust panel kernel on ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs.
claims.quote: To address the issue of numerical breakdown of LUC2 when the L-factor from LU factorization is ill-conditioned, we employ HouseholderQR ... we utilize HouseholderQR to generate the upper-triangular factor S in LU-CholeskyQR.

claims.claim: The method uses randomized sketching as a preconditioner to shrink the matrix the expensive HouseholderQR runs on: a single Gaussian sketch (SLHC3) or a two-stage CountSketch-then-Gaussian sketch (SSLHC3), with HouseholderQR applied only to the small sketched L (size s, not m), making the serial-Householder portion operate on a much smaller matrix — relevant to shortening the panel critical path.
claims.quote: By applying a Gaussian sketch after a CountSketch, we can achieve low computational and storage costs while leaving a matrix with a smaller size ... [H, S] = HouseholderQR(Ls)

claims.claim: rLHC outputs only the explicit orthogonal factor Q and upper-triangular R, NOT a flat geqrf-compatible (H, tau) Householder representation; the internal Householder vectors from the sketched-L step are discarded, so it does not directly satisfy the output contract requiring packed (H, tau) that compose as one global householder_product.
claims.quote: Orthogonal factor Q ∈ ℝᵐˣⁿ, Upper triangular factor R ∈ ℝⁿˣⁿ ... [the Householder vectors are not returned; only Q and R]

claims.claim: The paper's analysis and experiments are entirely double-precision CPU (unit roundoff u = 2^-53) with no GPU, tensor-core, TF32/tf32x3, or mixed-precision content and no wall-clock GPU timings — so its efficiency claims do not transfer directly to the B200 tensor-core panel-factorization problem and it is not a batched-QR method.
claims.quote: No GPU details mentioned ... unit roundoff 𝐮 = 2⁻⁵³ (double precision). No mention of TF32, FP32 variants, or mixed-precision arithmetic.

claims.claim: rand_cholQR (Randomized Householder-Cholesky QR) achieves orthogonality error bounded by O(unit roundoff) with high probability for ANY numerically full-rank matrix, removing CholeskyQR2's condition-number restriction — making it numerically robust on ill-conditioned inputs where naive CholeskyQR fails (which is exactly the robustness constraint the QR-panel task requires).
claims.quote: with high probability, its orthogonality error is bounded by a constant of the order of unit roundoff for any numerically full-rank matrix, and hence it is as stable as shifted CholeskyQR3.

claims.claim: rand_cholQR matches or beats CholeskyQR2 in speed on tall-and-skinny matrices while adding stability at almost no extra cost — relevant because the panel factorization (tall-skinny n x IB QR) is the critical-path bottleneck, and a sketch+Cholesky panel is GEMM-heavy (tensor-core friendly) rather than serial-reflector-bound.
claims.quote: For tall-and-skinny matrices, rand_cholQR with multiple sketch matrices is nearly as fast as, or in some cases faster than, CholeskyQR2.

claims.claim: The method uses one or two random sketch matrices (multisketching) to obtain stability comparable to shifted CholeskyQR3 at roughly CholeskyQR2 cost, i.e. it avoids the ~50% extra work of a third Cholesky pass.
claims.quote: more stable with almost no extra computational or memory cost

claims.claim: rand_cholQR's stability guarantee was demonstrated on an NVIDIA A100 GPU (not Blackwell/B200, and not in the flat-Householder (H,tau) output form required by the task's checker — it produces an explicit orthonormal Q, so adopting it for this task would require a separate Householder-reconstruction/ORHR_COL step to emit geqrf-compatible reflectors).
claims.quote: For tall-and-skinny matrices, rand_cholQR with multiple sketch matrices is nearly as fast as, or in some cases faster than, CholeskyQR2.

claims.claim: DORHR_COL implements Householder reconstruction: given an M-by-N matrix Q_in with orthonormal columns (e.g. from TSQR/CholeskyQR), it reconstructs Householder vectors V implicitly representing Q_out such that Q_in = Q_out * S, where S is an N-by-N diagonal ±1 sign matrix. This is exactly the cheap reconstruction step the research question asks about for emitting flat geqrf-compatible (H, tau) from a communication-avoiding factor.
claims.quote: DORHR_COL takes an M-by-N real matrix Q_in with orthonormal columns as input, stored in A, and performs Householder Reconstruction (HR), i.e. reconstructs Householder vectors V(i) implicitly representing another M-by-N matrix Q_out, with the property that Q_in = Q_out*S, where S is an N-by-N diagonal matrix with diagonal entries equal to +1 or -1.

claims.claim: The reconstruction is computed as a modified (sign-shifted) LU/Gaussian-elimination factorization: Q_in minus the sign matrix factors as V*U with V unit lower-trapezoidal and U upper-triangular, and the per-column sign is D(i) = -SIGN(Q_in_i(i,i)). This gives the exact recurrence for the reconstruction step and shows it is an LU-type (not another QR), which bounds its cost and structure.
claims.quote: D(i) is constructed as D(i) = -SIGN(Q_in_i(i,i)), where 1 <= i <= min(M,N)

claims.claim: DORHR_COL outputs block reflectors T in the same NB-by-NB upper-triangular format as DGEQRT, expressing Q_out as a product of compact-WY block reflectors Q_out(i) = I - VB(i)*TB(i)*VB(i)^T. This means the reconstructed representation is directly compatible with the standard blocked/compact-WY apply path (DGEMQRT), so the reconstruction can plug into a tensor-core GEMM trailing-update pipeline.
claims.quote: Q_out(i) = I - VB(i) * TB(i) * (VB(i))^T

claims.claim: The sign matrix S must be folded into R to keep the factorization valid: R_out = S * R_in (some rows of R negated). This is the required correctness fixup so the reconstructed flat (H, tau) plus R still satisfies A = Q*R for the checker, and it is an O(n^2)-per-matrix row scaling (cheap relative to the panel).
claims.quote: So if one wants to interpret Q_out as the result of the QR factorization of B, then the corresponding R_out should be equal to R_out = S * R_in, i.e. some rows of R_in should be multiplied by -1.

claims.claim: The algorithm is the Ballard-Demmel-Grigori et al. Householder-reconstruction-from-TSQR method, with the canonical citation being JPDC vol. 85, pp. 3-31, 2015, confirming this LAPACK routine is the production implementation of the exact paper named in the research question.
claims.quote: G. Ballard, J. Demmel, L. Grigori, M. Jacquelin, H.D. Nguyen, E. Solomonik, J. Parallel Distrib. Comput., vol. 85, pp. 3-31, 2015.

claims.claim: ChASE deliberately replaced Householder QR (HHQR) with communication-avoiding CholeskyQR variants for the tall-skinny orthogonalization, and chose CholeskyQR over TSQR specifically because CholeskyQR's reduction operator is addition while TSQR's is a QR factorization of a small matrix; TSQR only beats ScaLAPACK-HHQR in a 1D grid when m >> n. This bears on the research question's panel regime: for batched SQUARE-ish panels (n x IB where IB is modest, not m>>n), TSQR's tree-reduction advantage may be marginal, matching the question's grid-starved-but-not-extremely-tall shapes.
claims.quote: We preferred CholeskyQR rather than tall-skinny QR (TSQR) [4], a CAQR with equivalent communication costs as CholeskyQR, because the reduction operator of CholeskyQR is addition, while that of TSQR is the QR factorization of a small matrix [9]. To our knowledge, TSQR is advantageous over ScaLAPACK-HHQR in 1D MPI grid only if m >> n

claims.claim: Robust QR can be achieved by a condition-number-gated switch among three CholeskyQR variants with a Householder fallback: estimated kappa > O(u^-1/2) (~1e8 in double) selects shifted-CholeskyQR2 (s-CholeskyQR2, valid up to kappa ~ O(u^-1)); kappa < 20 uses a single CholeskyQR; otherwise CholeskyQR2 (run twice). A failed shifted Cholesky factorization (POTRF info != 0) reverts to ScaLAPACK-HHQR. This is a directly transferable template for the research question's robustness requirement (ill-conditioned / rank-deficient / near-collinear inputs), where naive single-pass CholeskyQR fails.
claims.quote: If the estimated condition number is larger than O (u −1/2 ), which is approximately 108 for double precision, we select the s-CholeskyQR2 variant. If the estimated condition number is smaller than a fixed threshold (in practice set to 20), CholeskyQR is sufficient. Otherwise, CholeskyQR2 should be used. To ensure robustness, we revert to HHQR in Algorithm 4 (Line 9) to prevent failures of s-CholeskyQR2 for any corner case.

claims.claim: The shifted-CholeskyQR2 stabilization adds an explicit diagonal shift sI before the Cholesky factorization, with shift s = 11*(m*n + n*(n+1))*u*||X||_F^2 (u = unit round-off), computed from the SYRK Gram matrix and the Frobenius norm; this preconditions an ill-conditioned X so Cholesky completes. This is a concrete, code-level recurrence the research question can adopt if a CholeskyQR-style fast path is used for the panel before reconstructing Householder vectors.
claims.quote: norm ←AllReduce ( ||X||F^2 , SUM, comm ) ... s = 11(mn + n (n + 1) )u·norm ... [R, info] ← POTRF(R + sI )

claims.claim: CholeskyQR loses orthogonality in Q as the condition number of X grows; running the algorithm twice (CholeskyQR2) significantly mitigates this, but CholeskyQR2 only works if the Gram matrix R = X^H X has a Cholesky factorization that runs to completion, requiring kappa_2(X) <= O(u^-1/2). This quantifies the exact numerical boundary at which the research question's ill-conditioned/clustered-singular-value test cases would break a plain CholeskyQR panel.
claims.quote: Despite the better performance, CholeskyQR is afflicted by a rapid decline in orthogonality across the columns of the Q factor for increasing condition number of X. This instability can be significantly mitigated by performing the algorithm twice, which is known as CholeskyQR2 [9]. The applicability of CholeskyQR2 is still limited by the requirement that the Cholesky factorization of the Gram matrix R = X^H X runs to completion, which requires the matrix X to have a condition number κ2(X) no larger than O (u −1/2 )

claims.claim: The CholeskyQR orthogonalization kernel is built entirely from GEMM-class BLAS3 primitives on GPU (SYRK to form the Gram matrix, POTRF for Cholesky, TRSM for back-substitution to get Q), offloaded via cuBLAS/cuSOLVER, with no serial reflector-by-reflector dependency chain. This is the key structural reason CholeskyQR avoids the panel critical-path bottleneck the research question identifies in Householder QR — but it emits an explicit Q (via TRSM), NOT flat (H, tau) reflectors, so it does not by itself satisfy the question's householder_product output contract.
claims.quote: For each repetition, it starts by partially calculating the Gram matrix X^H X on each MPI process, through LAPACK ZHERK (DSYRK) routines. The final Gram matrix is obtained via an AllReduce operation with addition. Then a Cholesky factorization is performed on R with LAPACK POTRF, and Q is computed via back substitution with the LAPACK TRSM.

claims.claim: Plain CholeskyQR2 (repeating CholeskyQR twice) is numerically stable only up to condition number ~10^8 (O(u^-1/2)); for kappa(A) > u^-1/2 the Gram matrix A^T A is not semi-positive-definite and the Cholesky factorization step breaks down, so naive CholeskyQR-family methods FAIL on ill-conditioned inputs. This bounds what condition number a squared-condition Gram-based panel can tolerate.
claims.quote: Although repeating CholeskyQR twice significantly improves orthogonality, CholeskyQR2 is still numerically unstable for ill-conditioned matrices with condition numbers greater than O(u^-1/2), where u is the unit roundoff. In practice, this means that the algorithm is stable up to condition numbers of 10^8 [12], [13], and the deviation from orthogonality of the computed Q is of order O(kappa(A)^2 u).

claims.claim: Robustness to extreme ill-conditioning (kappa up to 10^15-10^16) is recovered by interleaving CholeskyQR2 with block Gram-Schmidt re-orthogonalization so each trailing update uses a FULLY orthogonalized panel; the resulting orthogonality is equivalent to Householder-based QR (general and TSQR). This is the paper's mechanism for numerically-robust QR without Householder reflectors.
claims.quote: The main innovation of our approach lies in the interleaving of the CholeskyQR steps with the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation, which ensures that update steps are performed with fully orthogonalised panels. The obtained orthogonality and numerical stability of our modified algorithm is equivalent to CholeskyQR2 with Gram-Schmidt and other state-of-the-art methods.

claims.claim: Panel width b is the dominant tuning knob trading numerical stability against performance: narrower panels lower each panel's condition number (because condition number is the ratio of largest to smallest singular value, and removing columns shrinks it), enabling stability at high kappa; for kappa=10^15 the matrix must be split into ~10 panels (b=300 for n=3000) to reach orthogonality ~u, while kappa<10^8 needs only one panel. This panel-width-vs-conditioning tradeoff maps directly onto the batched-panel critical-path problem.
claims.quote: Too large b can lead to a large condition number of the Gram matrix Wj := Aj^T Aj and to numerical instability of the Cholesky factorization (see Fig.3). For an ill-conditioned matrix with kappa(A) = 10^15, the block size should be very small (b = 300) to achieve the orthogonality of order u resulting in dividing the matrix into a larger number of panels (concretely 10) and iterating over lines 2-10... On the other hand, for smaller condition numbers, the panel width is increased and the number of iterations is decreased.

claims.claim: A mixed-precision CholeskyQR variant (Yamazaki-Tomov-Dongarra 2015) keeps inputs/outputs in working precision while computing certain intermediate results in DOUBLED precision, making the orthogonality error depend only LINEARLY (not quadratically) on the condition number; the cost is a significant increase in floating-point instruction count. This is a concrete mixed-precision recipe relevant to keeping FP32-accurate panel reflectors on ill-conditioned inputs.
claims.quote: Since the orthogonality error of CholeskyQR depends quadratically on the condition number, the authors in [18] have proposed a mixed-precision approach. In this approach, the input and output matrices are retained in their required precision, while certain intermediate results are calculated at doubled precision. The analysis has shown that the orthogonality error of the mixed-precision CholeskyQR approach has a linear dependence on the condition number when doubled precision is used.

claims.claim: Randomized Householder-Cholesky QR with multisketching (Higgins-Szyld-Boman-Yamazaki 2023) bounds orthogonality error by a constant of order unit roundoff for matrices of ARBITRARY condition number using up to two random sketch matrices, and was reported faster than CholeskyQR2 while more stable than shifted CholeskyQR3. This is a distinct sketch-based route to condition-number-independent robust QR.
claims.quote: The most recent improvements to the orthogonality and stability of the CholeskyQR model was proposed in [17] with the so-called Randomised Householder-Cholesky QR Factorization with Multisketching. The proposed solution introduces up to two randomised sketch matrices (multisketching), which prove that the orthogonality error is bounded by a constant of the order of unit roundoff for matrices of arbitrary condition number.

claims.claim: Householder vectors can be reconstructed from the TSQR-computed orthonormal Q by performing an LU decomposition WITHOUT pivoting of (Q - S), where S is a diagonal sign matrix; the unit-lower-triangular L factor IS the packed Householder Y. This is exactly the ORHR_COL recurrence the research question seeks (item 1/2).
claims.quote: performing Householder-QR on an orthonormal matrix Q is the same as performing an LU decomposition on Q S, where S is a diagonal sign matrix corresponding to the sign choices made inside the Householder-QR algorithm

claims.claim: The reconstruction needs NO pivoting because the trailing matrix stays orthonormal, so the effective diagonal is >=1 and off-diagonals are <=1 in modulus throughout — this makes the LU a clean, parallelizable, GEMM-friendly factorization rather than a serial pivoted one.
claims.quote: with the choice of S, no pivoting is required since the e↵ective diagonal entry will be at least 1 in absolute value and all other entries in the column are bounded by 1 (the matrix is orthonormal). This holds true throughout the entire factorization because the trailing matrix remains orthonormal

claims.claim: The Householder representation is recovered from TSQR for roughly the same cost as TSQR itself, with little extra computation — directly answering whether the reconstruction can be made CHEAP rather than O(batch*n^3): the dominant term is the 4mb^2/p matmul, and the reconstruction-specific extra operations are only O(b^3).
claims.quote: the standard Householder vector representation may be recovered from the implicit TSQR representation for roughly the same cost as the TSQR itself

claims.claim: The reconstruction is provably as numerically stable as Householder-QR, INDEPENDENT of the matrix condition number (the LU growth factor is bounded by 2) — so it survives the ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs that break Cholesky-QR-based shortcuts. The cheaper LU(A-R) and Cholesky-QR variants are explicitly flagged as NOT as stable.
claims.quote: We prove in Section 4 that this reconstruction is as numerically stable as Householder-QR (independent of the matrix condition number)

claims.claim: The compact-WY T factor can be computed cheaply and stably directly from the LU upper-triangular factor (rather than re-deriving it from the Householder vectors), letting the method emit a blocked/compact-WY-applicable representation at low cost — useful for the existing blocked compact-WY pipeline.
claims.quote: we can stably compute the T̃ factor (needed to apply a blocked Householder update) from the upper triangular LU factor, a computationally cheaper method than using the Householder vectors themselves

claims.claim: CQRRPT, a randomized-preconditioned CholeskyQR for tall matrices, claims comparable performance to specialized communication-avoiding unpivoted-QR algorithms (shifted CholeskyQR3 and TSQR) while being more amenable to massively-parallel optimization, because its dominant cost is BLAS-3 GEMM plus one random projection (only two sum-reduce exchanges in distributed memory). This is the GEMM-heavy, TSQR-competitive panel alternative the research question asks about, but it produces an explicit Q (not flat H,tau).
claims.quote: CQRRPT can outperform not only other QRCP algorithms but also specialized communication-avoiding algorithms for unpivoted QR, such as shifted CholeskyQR3 [FKN+20] and TSQR [DGHL12]. The dominant cost of our algorithm is attributed exclusively to BLAS 3 operations and a random projection, rendering it highly efficient from a communication standpoint... compared to TSQR, CQRRPT lends itself more easily to performance optimization on massively parallel architectures, thanks to its simple reduction operator.

claims.claim: Plain CholeskyQR loses orthogonality as O(u*kappa(M)^2) and CholeskyQR2 (reorthogonalization, i.e. running CholeskyQR twice) still FAILS once kappa(M) > u^{-1/2}. For FP32 (u ~ 6e-8), u^{-1/2} ~ 4000, so naive/CholeskyQR2 panels break on the ill-conditioned inputs in the test set — confirming the research question's premise that naive CholeskyQR is unsafe and quantifying the exact condition-number cliff.
claims.quote: rounding errors can lead to significant orthogonality loss, in the sense that ∥Q∗Q − I∥2 can be as large as O(u κ(M)2 ). ... Another approach to mitigating orthogonality loss involves reorthogonalization (essentially running CholeskyQR twice) resulting in "CholeskyQR2". However, this method can still fail when κ(M) > u−1/2 .

claims.claim: Randomized preconditioning fixes the conditioning: sketch M (Msk = SM), QR the small sketch to get Rsk, form the preconditioned Mpre = M*Rsk^{-1}, and then CholeskyQR on Mpre is well-conditioned because under a delta-embedding (delta <= 1/2) the preconditioned condition number is bounded near 1 (kappa(Mpre) <= 1.8). The added cost over plain CholeskyQR is only ~mn^2 flops (leading term 3mn^2 vs 2mn^2). This is the cheap, GEMM-only recipe to make a CholeskyQR-style panel numerically robust on ill-conditioned inputs.
claims.quote: 1. Compute Msk = SM using a sketching operator S ∈ Rd×m with n ≤ d ≤ m. 2. Compute [Qsk , Rsk ] = qr(Msk ) and discard Qsk . 3. Form Mpre = M(Rsk )−1 explicitly, using back substitution. 4. Compute G = (Msk )∗ (Msk ) and Rpre = chol(G, "upper"). 5. Set Q = Mpre (Rpre )−1 and R = Rpre Rsk ... If a fast sketching operator is used with n ≤ d ≤ m, then the leading term in the resulting algorithm's flop count will be 3mn2 , which is only mn2 more than the standard CholeskyQR.

claims.claim: The numerically dominant step (forming the preconditioned matrix / Q-factor on Line 5) can be computed in LOWER precision than the rest while still keeping orthogonality loss near machine precision — the paper's two-unit-roundoff analysis proves stability holds for multi-/low-precision architectures. This directly supports a mixed-precision panel: do the expensive bulk in TF32/FP32 and only the small correction in higher precision, matching the research question's tf32x3 / mixed-precision robust-QR ask.
claims.quote: We have chosen a computational model with two unit roundoffs to highlight an important property of the preconditioner – that the dominant Line 5 can be performed with a [lower precision]... into multi- or low-precision arithmetic architectures. Clearly, the numerical stability of CQRRPT computed with two unit roundoffs also implies its stability when computed with [a single roundoff].

claims.claim: CholeskyQR/CQRRPT returns an EXPLICIT Q-factor (Q = M*R^{-1}), whereas GEQRF returns an implicit Householder representation; converting GEQRF's implicit factor to explicit Q via ORGQR costs an extra ~2mn^2-(2/3)n^3 flops. This is the cautionary inverse of the research question's need: the contract requires flat (H,tau), so a CQRRPT-style panel would need a Householder-reconstruction (ORHR_COL) step ON TOP — the paper confirms the explicit<->implicit conversion is itself an O(mn^2) GEMM-cost, not free.
claims.quote: CholeskyQR returns an explicit Q-factor, while GEQRF outputs an implicit representation of its Q-factor... Translating GEQRF's implicit factor into an explicit form (using LAPACK's ORGQR) takes an additional 2mn2 − (2/3)n3 flops [ADO94, Page 122].

result.publishDate: 2025-03-16 (v3; original v1 Nov 2023). Accepted at SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. (SIMAX).

claims.claim: CAQR's TSQR panel factorization replaces the serial reflector chain with a tree reduction over vertical row-blocks, mapped one-thread-block-per-block on the GPU, which exposes the parallelism needed to fill idle SMs at grid-starved (tall-skinny) sizes.
claims.quote: Instead of computing one Householder [vector for the whole column we divide the] matrix vertically into small blocks... in our application each small block QR decomposition is done by a different thread block.

claims.claim: The decisive panel-kernel optimization is keeping the small-block matrix entirely in the register file with serial (per-thread) reductions plus a panel transpose, which raised the core apply-Q^T kernel from 55 GFLOPS (naive shared-memory parallel reduction) to 388 GFLOPS — a ~7x gain attributed to avoiding shared memory/L1 in favor of registers.
claims.quote: we were able to improve the performance of apply qt h, our main kernel, from 55 GFLOPS to 388 GFLOPS using low-level tuning... The most important tuning optimization was to avoid shared memory and L1 cache in favor of the register file.

claims.claim: Doing TSQR within the column panel removes the synchronization of standard blocked Householder and lets the trailing-matrix update begin before the panel is fully factored, shortening the critical path / exposing look-ahead parallelism.
claims.quote: the trailing matrix update can begin before the entire panel is factored. This removes the synchronization in the standard blocked Householder approach and exposes more [parallelism].

claims.claim: On the GPU the reduction tree is a quad-tree (vs. the binomial tree used in prior multicore CAQR): with 64x16 blocks the panel height shrinks by 4 per level, and the tree stops once the panel height is under 64 so it fits one thread block.
claims.quote: binomial tree reduction was used [10], whereas our GPU approach employs a quad-tree reduction... we reduce the height of the panel by a factor of 4 at each level... The tree reduction ends when the panel height becomes less than 64, meaning it can be processed completely in a single thread block.

claims.claim: CAQR produces the standard SGEQRF intermediate Householder representation (not explicit Q), and retrieving Q explicitly via SORGQR is reported as just as efficient as the factorization — relevant to emitting a flat (H, tau)-style representation cheaply; however the implementation is single-precision-only and validated only on a well-conditioned video application, so it does not address ill-conditioned/rank-deficient robustness.
claims.quote: This routine doesn't return Q explicitly, instead it returns an intermediate representation that can later be used to retreive or apply Q. Though not shown on the graph, retreiving Q explicitly (SORGQR) using CAQR is just as efficient as factoring the matrix.

claims.claim: Householder vectors can be reconstructed from TSQR's implicit Q by a SINGLE modified-LU decomposition (no pivoting) of the explicit Q factor minus a diagonal sign matrix S: running LU on Q-S yields exactly the Householder Y (unit lower triangular) and U, from which T = -U S Y1^{-T} via one b x b triangular solve. This directly answers the research question's item 1 (cheap reconstruction emitting flat geqrf-compatible Y,T) and item 2 (TSQR + ORHR_COL). The key recurrence is Modified-LU Algorithm 5: S(i,i)=-sgn(Q(i,i)); subtract from diagonal; scale column by 1/Q(i,i); Schur-complement update Q(i+1:m,i+1:b) -= Q(i+1:m,i)*Q(i,i+1:b).
claims.quote: The key idea of our reconstruction algorithm is that performing Householder-QR on an orthonormal matrix Q is the same as performing an LU decomposition on Q - S, where S is a diagonal sign matrix... if Q = I - Y T Y1^T with Y a matrix of Householder vectors, then Y * (-T Y1^T) is an LU decomposition of Q - I since Y is unit lower triangular and T Y1^T is upper triangular.

claims.claim: The reconstruction is CHEAP and GEMM/BLAS-3-heavy, not O(batch*n^3): Construct-TSQR-Q incurs the SAME flop/communication cost as TSQR itself, and the full TSQR-HR panel (TSQR + reconstruct + T) costs only 5mb^2/p flops vs 3mb^2/p for Householder-QR (Table 1) -- i.e. ~1.67x the panel flops but with the same asymptotic communication and far lower latency (4 log p vs 2b log p messages). The dominant work is the (m/p)b^2 apply and triangular solves; the serial part is just one b x b LU plus a b x b triangular solve that overlaps the column update. This is exactly the 'reconstruction itself can be tensor-core GEMM-heavy and parallel' the question asks for.
claims.quote: we can reconstruct the unique part of the Q matrix from the implicit form given by TSQR for the same cost as the TSQR itself.

claims.claim: TSQR-HR is provably as numerically stable as standard Householder-QR, independent of condition number -- the backward error and loss of orthogonality (Theorem 5.5: ||A - QR||_F <= F1*||A||_F and ||I - Q^T Q||_F <= F2) are bounded by O(b*gamma*sqrt(m)) terms with NO dependence on kappa(A). Empirically (Table 3, 5) errors stay ~1e-15 in FP64 across well-known anomalous and very ill-conditioned matrices. This directly satisfies the research question's robustness requirement (ill-conditioned / rank-deficient / clustered-singular-value inputs must not blow up). No-pivoting is safe because the diagonal of Q-S is >=1 and off-diagonals <=1 (orthonormality), preserved throughout.
claims.quote: for all test cases both the orthogonality and factorization errors of are of order 10-15 for TSQR-HR, which is close to  = 2-52 of double precision... TSQR-HR is numerically stable in terms of backward errors when computing the QR factorization of full matrices, regardless of the condition number of the matrix, as suggested by Theorem 5.5.

claims.claim: The naive cheap alternative -- reconstructing Householder vectors via LU(A-R) (LU of the original matrix minus R, with T from Y^T Y) -- is UNSTABLE: backward errors grow with the condition number of the matrix and are unsatisfactory. This is a falsifiable warning bearing on the research question's item 5/6: a tempting shortcut to flat (H,tau) that skips the explicit-Q construction will FAIL the ill-conditioned test cases, whereas the Modified-LU-on-Q path (or Yamamoto's basis-kernel) remains stable. The orthonormality of Q is what makes the LU pivot-free and stable; A is not orthonormal so LU(A-R) loses it.
claims.quote: the LU(A - R) method provides unsatisfactory backward errors which grow with the condition number of the matrix.

claims.claim: TSQR replaces the serial column-by-column reflector chain with a tree reduction over row blocks (one reduction per column for Householder-QR becomes a single tree of height log p), and Yamamoto's dense basis-kernel representation Q = I - Y~ T~ Y~^T with Y~=[Q1-S; Q2], T~ = (I-Q1)-block-inverse is an equivalent stable alternative obtained from the same explicit Q via two triangular solves (Y = Y~ U^{-1}, T = U L^{-T}). This bears on items 2 and 6: the tree structure fills idle SMs at grid-starved batch, and either reconstruction (Modified-LU or Yamamoto) converts the implicit tree-Q into a flat block reflector applicable as one GEMM -- the choice is a cheap-experiment knob (Yamamoto skips the Q2 triangular solve).
claims.quote: TSQR... overcomes this bottleneck by reformulating the computation. In fact, the algorithm is communication optimal... the Householder basis-kernel representation in Equation (2) can be obtained from the representation given in Equation (3) with two triangular solves: if the LU factorization gives I - Q1 = LU, then Y = Y~ U^{-1} and T = U L^{-T}.

claims.claim: Static look-ahead removes the sequential panel factorization from the critical path by software-pipelining: the trailing update is split into TU^L (leftmost b columns, which exactly overlap PF_{k+1}) and TU^R, and PF_{k+1} is executed in the SAME iteration as the current trailing update, overlapping the serial panel factorization of the next panel with the highly-parallel update of the current trailing submatrix. This is the concrete recurrence to shorten the panel critical path (research item 3).
claims.quote: The trailing update is broken into two panels/suboperations/tasks only, TU_k -> (TU_k^L | TU_k^R), where TU_k^L contains the leftmost b columns of TU_k, which exactly overlap those of PF_{k+1}. The algorithm is then (manually) re-organized, applying a sort of software pipelining in order to perform the panel factorization PF_{k+1} in the same iteration as the update

claims.claim: The panel factorization is mostly sequential and, as core count grows, the relative cost of the highly-parallel trailing update shrinks, transforming the largely-sequential panel into the major performance bottleneck that must be overlapped with the trailing update. This confirms the research question's premise that the panel is the critical path once the trailing GEMM is at roofline.
claims.quote: The panel factorization, in contrast, is mostly sequential and needs to be overlapped with the trailing update to prevent it from becoming a bottleneck for the performance of the global algorithm.

claims.claim: The look-ahead variant restructures the loop so each iteration calls PU(k+1) = combined left trailing update TU_k^L plus next panel factorization PF_{k+1}, and TU_right(k) = the right trailing update TU_k^R; an initial PF(0) is done before the loop. This is the exact loop skeleton (Listing 5) for emitting the pipelined schedule.

For the dense factorizations the panel width b should be small (a few hundred columns; b=192 used to match the BLIS micro-kernel k_c) so that most computation is cast as the compute-intensive trailing update GEMM rather than the panel. This bounds the panel cost relative to the trailing update via the block size.
claims.quote: For high performance, the width of the panel (i.e., its number of columns, b) is in general set to a small value (a few hundreds) in order to cast most computations in terms of the compute-intensive trailing update.

claims.claim: The look-ahead/RTM strategy decomposes the k-th trailing update into multiple column-panel sub-updates TU_k -> (TU_k^{k+1} | TU_k^{k+2} | TU_k^{k+3}...) and overlaps their modification with future panel factorizations; static look-ahead is preferred over dynamic because it is applied at the algorithm level rather than via a runtime, and the dependency structure forms a DAG (Figure 3) where PF_{k+1} depends only on TU_k^L. This DAG is the schedule a GPU implementation would replicate to fill idle SMs during the panel.
claims.quote: RTM-LU overcomes this problem by introducing a sort of dynamic look-ahead strategy that can overlap the execution of the “future” panel factorization(s) with that of the “current” trailing update

claims.claim: A recursive QR factorization algorithm replaces the Level 2 BLAS portion of the standard block QR (the panel/'factorization part') with Level 3 BLAS operations, via automatic variable blocking from the recursion — directly addressing the panel-factorization bottleneck where the serial reflector chain is Level-2-bound.
claims.quote: The recursion leads to an automatic variable blocking and replaces a Level 2 part in a standard block algorithm with Level 3 operations.

claims.claim: The hybrid recursive QR algorithm outperforms LAPACK's DGEQRF by about 20% for large square matrices and by up to almost a factor of 3 for tall-thin matrices, quantifying the achievable panel speedup from recursion.
claims.quote: A hybrid recursive algorithm is introduced that outperforms the LAPACK algorithm DGEQRF by about 20% for large square matrices and up to almost a factor of 3 for tall thin matrices.

claims.claim: Recursion improves QR performance MOST for tall-thin matrices — exactly the n x IB panel shape that is the critical-path bottleneck in the research question — because the standard LAPACK code computes that factorization part as Level 2 while recursion makes it Level 3.
claims.quote: The main result of the paper shows that recursion improves performance most for tall thin matrices.

claims.claim: The recursive formulation automatically blocks for the memory hierarchy, removing the need for a hand-tuned fixed panel/block width and instead producing variable-width sub-panels down the recursion tree (the geqrt3-style divide-and-conquer panel later adopted by PLASMA/LAPACK).
claims.quote: The recursive algorithms automatically block for the memory hierarchy and produce a Level 3 implementation of the "factorization part of the code," whereas LAPACK implementations compute this part as Level 2.

claims.claim: Selectively using doubled precision only at the Gram-matrix and Cholesky steps reduces the orthogonality error of Cholesky QR from quadratic to LINEAR in the input condition number (O(d*kappa(V)) instead of O(d*kappa(V)^2)), making CholQR usable on ill-conditioned inputs that would otherwise fail. This is the falsifiable robustness mechanism for the project's prohibition on naive CholeskyQR.
claims.quote: Our analysis shows that by selectively using the doubled precision, the orthogonality error of the mixed-precision CholQR only depends linearly on the condition number of the input matrix. [...] Theorem 3.3. If the doubled precision is used for the first two steps of CholQR, and d is the machine epsilon in the working precision (i.e., 1 = 2 = 2d and 3 = d ), then we have I - Q^T Q <= O(d kappa(V) + (d kappa(V))^2) [...] In particular, with our assumption made at Step 2 of CholQR (i.e., kappa(V) <= eps_d^{-1}), we have I - Q^T Q <= O(d kappa(V)) and Q = O(1).

claims.claim: The higher precision is needed ONLY at Step 1 (Gram matrix B := V^T V) and Step 2 (Cholesky factorization R^T R := B); Step 3 (the triangular solve / forward substitution Q := V R^-1) stays in the working precision. This is the precise, cheap recipe for where to spend the extra precision (analogous to TF32->FP32 accumulation only in reflector/Gram formation, not the apply).
claims.quote: For the remainder of the paper, we focus on the mixed-precision CholQR which uses the doubled precision at the first two steps of CholQR, while using the working precision at the last step.

claims.claim: Software-emulated doubled precision (double-double / Cray-style) costs about 8.5x more floating-point instructions than standard CholQR, yet on a (2015-era) latest NVIDIA GPU the mixed-precision CholQR was only ~1.4x slower than standard, because the kernel is communication/round-bound rather than flop-bound and the higher-precision data volume increase is small (n << m). This bounds the real cost of an emulated-precision (e.g. tf32x3/3xTF32) panel/Gram step.
claims.quote: using software-emulated double-double precision for the working 64-bit double precision, the mixed-precision CholQR requires about 8.5x more floating-point instructions than that required by the standard CholQR. On the other hand, the increase in the communication cost using the double-double precision is less significant [...] As a result, with a latest NVIDIA GPU, the mixed-precision CholQR was only 1.4x slower than the standard CholQR.

claims.claim: A direct properties table contrasts the orthogonalization schemes on GPUs: CholQR and SVQR have orthogonality error O(kappa(V)^2) with BLAS-3 xGEMM and O(1) messages; Householder-based CAQR has error O(eps) (condition-independent) but its dominant kernel is BLAS-1/2 xGEQF2 (the serial-reflector panel), costs 4n^2*m flops (2x CholQR), and O(1) messages. This quantifies exactly the CholQR-speed-vs-Householder-stability tradeoff and pins the panel cost to BLAS-1/2 GEQF2.
claims.quote: MGS O(kappa(V)) ... CGS O(kappa(V) n^-1) ... CholQR O(kappa(V)^2) 2n^2 m BLAS-3 xGEMM O(1) ... SVQR O(kappa(V)^2) 2n^2 m BLAS-3 xGEMM O(1) ... CAQR O(eps) 4n^2 m BLAS-1,2 xGEQF2 O(1)

claims.claim: Mixed-precision CholQR is only valid when the Cholesky factorization succeeds, which requires the squared condition number to stay below the reciprocal of the doubled-precision epsilon (kappa(V)^2 <= eps_2^-1); when V is ill-conditioned or rank-deficient the Cholesky can fail outright, in which case SVQR (SVD of the Gram matrix) is the robust fallback. This bounds how near-rank-deficient an input the method can handle before needing an SVD/re-orthogonalization fallback.
claims.quote: we assume in this paper that the condition number of B is less than the reciprocal of the machine precision used at Step 2 (i.e., kappa(B) <= eps_2^-1 or, equivalently, kappa(V)^2 <= eps_2^-1). [...] when the matrix V is ill-conditioned, or one of the column vectors vj is a linear combination of the other columns, the Cholesky factorization of the Gram matrix may fail, while SVQR overcomes this numerical challenge.
