claims.claim: geqrt3 (xGEQRT3) recursively computes a QR factorization of an M-by-N matrix using the compact WY representation H = I - V*T*V^T, where V holds the reflector vectors and T is a small upper-triangular matrix encoding the block reflector — i.e. it produces a flat geqrf-compatible (V, T) representation, not per-panel reflectors that fail to compose, making it directly applicable to the panel-factorization critical path.
claims.quote: DGEQRT3 recursively computes a QR factorization of a general real or complex matrix using the compact WY representation of Q.

claims.claim: The recursion shortens the serial Householder dependency chain by divide-and-conquer: it splits the N columns into N1=N/2 and N2=N-N1, recursively factors the left block A(1:M,1:N1) -> (Y1,R1,T1), applies Q1^H to the right block A(1:M,J1:N), then recursively factors the lower-right block A(J1:M,J1:N) -> (Y2,R2,T2). This replaces a length-N serial reflector-by-reflector loop with a log-depth recursion whose internal updates are TRMM/GEMM (tensor-core-mappable), addressing the panel critical path without communication-avoiding tree reduction.
claims.quote: N1 = N/2 ... N2 = N-N1 ... CALL DGEQRT3( M, N1, A, LDA, T, LDT, IINFO ) ... CALL DGEQRT3( M-N1, N2, A( J1, J1 ), LDA, T( J1, J1 ), LDT, IINFO )

claims.claim: The two sub-panel T factors are combined into one global T via the off-diagonal block recurrence T3 = T(1:N1,J1:N) = -T1 * (Y1^H * Y2) * T2, computed with TRMM and GEMM. This is the exact cheap, GEMM-heavy merge formula needed to fuse two independently-factored sub-panels into a SINGLE compact-WY (V,T) that composes as one global householder_product sequence — the key to emitting flat (H,tau) after a divide step.
claims.quote: Compute T3 = T(1:N1,J1:N) = -T1 Y1^H Y2 T2

claims.claim: Applying the left sub-block's reflector Q1^H to the right columns inside the recursion is itself done as dense BLAS-3 (DTRMM + DGEMM) on the workspace block T(1:N1,J1:N), demonstrating that the inter-sub-panel coupling of the divide-and-conquer panel is tensor-core GEMM work rather than serial vector operations.
claims.quote: Compute A(1:M,J1:N) = Q1^H A(1:M,J1:N) [workspace: T(1:N1,J1:N)]" followed by matrix operations involving DTRMM and DGEMM

claims.claim: The paper's algorithm (mCQRGSI+) is NOT Householder-based: it is a CholeskyQR + block Gram-Schmidt method that explicitly outputs the factored Q (orthogonal) and R (upper triangular), and deliberately AVOIDS TSQR/Householder. It therefore does NOT emit a flat (H, tau) Householder-reflector representation and is not directly compatible with the research question's householder_product output contract.
claims.quote: Notably, mCQRGSI+ achieves stability without resorting to TSQR or other unconditionally stable Householder-based QR variants, which typically incur higher communication overheads and increased computational cost. ... Output: Q in R^{m x n} orthogonal and R in R^{n x n} upper triangular matrix

claims.claim: CholeskyQR's loss of orthogonality scales as O(eps)*kappa^2(A), so the Gram matrix A^T A squares the condition number and the Cholesky step FAILS for ill-conditioned inputs -- confirming that naive/batched CholeskyQR cannot pass the research question's ill-conditioned/rank-deficient test cases. The robustness fix is to keep each PANEL's condition number small enough that O(eps)*kappa^2(A_j) < 1 (kappa(A_j) < ~1e8 in FP64), which the panel-width choice controls.
claims.quote: The loss of orthogonality increases with the condition number of the input matrix A and is upper bounded by O(eps)kappa^2(A) [18] ... Since the matrix multiplication squares the condition number, the resulting Gram matrix may not be positive definite for very ill-conditioned matrices, causing the Cholesky factorisation step to fail. ... this condition requires that the condition number of each panel is small enough (<10^8 in double precision arithmetic) to ensure the numerical stability of the inner CholeskyQR (CQR) routine.

claims.claim: Numerical robustness for extreme conditioning (kappa up to 1e16) is achieved purely by a two-pass reorthogonalization skeleton (BMGS on the trailing submatrix for stability, then CQR to precondition the panel to kappa~1, then BCGS against the left panels in a single step) plus repeated inner CholeskyQR -- a re-orthogonalization recipe that achieves O(eps) loss of orthogonality comparable to Householder QR without any Householder reflectors. This re-orthogonalization pattern is directly transferable to making a robust panel factorization for rank-deficient/ill-conditioned inputs.
claims.quote: the robust Block Modified Gram-Schmidt (BMGS) is applied to ensure stability during this critical phase. Subsequently, an initial pass of CQR is applied to the current panel (line 6). While this does not guarantee full orthogonality of the computed matrix Q_j, it significantly improves its condition number, making it nearly orthogonal (kappa ~ 1). Because the panel is now well-conditioned, the second reorthogonalisation step (lines 7-8) can safely employ the more efficient Block Classical Gram-Schmidt (BCGS) ... mCQRGSI+ successfully maintains numerical stability close to machine precision for matrices with condition numbers as high as 10^16.

claims.claim: The paper provides a counter-data-point to the TSQR-on-GPU direction: it argues TSQR/CAQR for tall-and-skinny panels still performs a large fraction of flops in memory-bound Level-1/Level-2 BLAS to orthogonalize the local leaf blocks, and that CholeskyQR has roughly HALF the arithmetic cost of TSQR while expressing all steps as Level-3 BLAS. This warns that a TSQR leaf factorization may itself be BLAS-1/2 bound (the same panel bottleneck the question is trying to escape).
claims.quote: Although the degree of parallelism is significantly increased compared to traditional Householder QR, a large number of flops are still performed in memory-bound Level-1 and Level-2 BLAS kernels to orthogonalise the local blocks. ... CholeskyQR (CQR) is a simple algorithm with very low communication overhead and approximately half the arithmetic cost of TSQR

claims.claim: The work is distributed multi-GPU FP64 on NVIDIA A100 (CUDA 12.5), NOT single-GPU batched and NOT Blackwell/tensor-core/TF32; all routines run strictly in double precision. Speedups reported are 16x over SLATE CholeskyQR2 on GPUs and up to 12x over ScaLAPACK PDGEQRF (incl. PDORGQR) on CPUs -- relative to distributed library baselines, not to a tuned single-GPU batched kernel, so the magnitudes do not transfer to the B200 batched-QR setting.
claims.quote: supported by four NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPUs with 40 GB of device memory each. ... All codes were compiled with CMake 3.26.0 using gcc 11.2.1, CUDA 12.5 ... all computational routines were performed strictly in double-precision arithmetic ... outperforming the Householder-based QR factorisation from ScaLAPACK by a factor of 12 on distributed CPU systems and the CholeskyQR2 implementation from the SLATE library by up to 16x on GPU systems.

claims.claim: Shifted CholeskyQR adds a shift sI to the Gram matrix before Cholesky factorization, with the analyzed shift s = 11{mn + n(n+1)}·u·||X||_2^2 (and in practice the much smaller s = u·||X||_2^2 suffices), guaranteeing the factorization R^T R = A^T A + sI does not break down for ill-conditioned matrices. This is the direct fix for the research question's warning that naive CholeskyQR fails on ill-conditioned inputs — it makes a Gram-based panel factorization numerically safe.
claims.quote: as in Cholesky QR we compute the Gram matrix, but add a small shift sI so as to guarantee the Cholesky factorization RTR = ATA + sI does not break down ... 11{mn +n(n + 1)}u∥X∥2 ... much smaller shift, such as s =O(u∥A∥2), is usually suﬃcient to avoid breakdown

claims.claim: Vanilla CholeskyQR2 is numerically valid only for condition number kappa_2(X) <~ u^(-1/2); shifted CholeskyQR extends the safe range to kappa_2(X) = O(u^(-1)) (one shifted step yields AR^{-1} with reduced condition number <= u^(-1/2)). For FP32 (u~6e-8) this caps the method at kappa ~ 1e7, which is the hard ceiling for the near-rank-deficient / clustered-singular-value test inputs in the research question.
claims.quote: In this work we extend the applicability to κ2(X) = O(u−1) ... AR−1 (note that R−1 is also triangular) has reduced condition number ≤ u− 1 2

claims.claim: shiftedCholeskyQR3 attains backward-stable accuracy by running Cholesky QR three times, achieving both orthogonality ||Q^T Q - I||_2 and residual ||A - QR||_F/||A||_F at the O(u) level. This is the robustness target the flat-(H,tau) output must meet (checker requires O(eps32) orthogonality and residual), showing a Gram-based panel can in principle reach FP32 accuracy without Householder.
claims.quote: by essentially running Cholesky QR thrice ... ‖Q^T Q - I‖₂ and residual ‖A - QR‖_F/‖A‖_F both O(u)

claims.claim: Cholesky QR (and its shifted variant) is communication-avoiding with communication cost equivalent to TSQR but is rich in BLAS-3 (matrix-multiply / Gram-matrix and trailing GEMM) operations, so it typically runs faster than TSQR and offers ample parallelism. This is directly relevant to the panel-bottleneck goal: it replaces the serial Householder reflector chain with tensor-core GEMM-heavy BLAS-3 work, fitting the B200 TF32 tensor-core target.
claims.quote: Cholesky QR is a communication-avoiding algorithm whose communication cost is equivalent to that of the TSQR ... it is rich in BLAS-3 operations, and oﬀers ample opportunity for parallelization

claims.claim: Achieving robustness at extreme conditioning via double-double (3xTF32-style emulated) precision in the Gram and GEMM steps costs about 8.5x the arithmetic operations of plain CholeskyQR. This quantifies the price of mixed-precision error-corrected accumulation for the panel — relevant to the tf32x3/3xTF32 emulation option in the research question and its compute-cost tradeoff.

claims.claim: Householder vectors can be reconstructed from a known R by an LU-without-pivoting step: forming Q (the orthonormal factor from TSQR) and running Modified-LU (Algorithm 3) on Q·S yields the lower-triangular factor L which IS exactly the Householder Y matrix, with the sign matrix S computed on-the-fly as S(i,i)=sgn(Q(i,i)). No pivoting is ever needed because the trailing matrix stays orthonormal (diagonal >= 1, off-diagonals <= 1). This is the exact recurrence the research question asks for (ORHR_COL).
claims.quote: Ignoring lines 2 and 3, Algorithm 3 is exactly LU decomposition without pivoting. Note that with the choice of S, no pivoting is required since the effective diagonal entry will be at least 1 in absolute value and all other entries in the column are bounded by 1 (the matrix is orthonormal)... The lower triangular output L is exactly the Householder vector matrix Y.

claims.claim: The reconstruction is GEMM/BLAS3-heavy and cheap: the T factor of the compact-WY form is obtained from the upper-triangular LU output U via a triangular solve (T = U S^{-1} Y1^{-T}) rather than from Y^T Y, and the whole pipeline is (1) TSQR, (2) Modified-LU on Q, (3) compute T from U, (4) output A=(I-YTY1^T)(SR). All extra steps beyond TSQR are O(b^3) (the panel-width cube), confirming reconstruction adds only low-order cost over the trailing-update GEMMs.
claims.quote: we can compute T = U S^{-1} Y1^{-T} using triangular solve with multiple right hand sides rather than computing it from Y^T Y... All these additional operations are performed on processor 0 and their flop counts are O(b^3).

claims.claim: The reconstruction step costs essentially nothing asymptotically relative to the work it replaces: Table 1 gives full TSQR-HR at 4mb^2/p + (4b^3/3) log p flops versus plain TSQR at 2mb^2/p + (2b^3/3) log p, i.e. reconstruction (plus applying Q to the triangle and forming T) only doubles the leading mb^2 term and adds an O(b^3 log p) term — it does NOT add an O(mb^2)-per-reflector serial cost. This directly answers 'can the reconstruction be made cheap': yes, its overhead over TSQR is low-order in the panel width b.
claims.quote: We show how to perform TSQR and then reconstruct the Householder vector representation with the same asymptotic communication efficiency and little extra computational cost.

claims.claim: Reconstruction is provably as numerically stable as Householder-QR, INDEPENDENT of matrix condition number, because Modified-LU runs on an orthonormal (perfectly conditioned) matrix so the LU growth factor is bounded by 2 and no pivoting is needed. Lemma 4.4 bounds the backward error of the reconstructed (Y,T,S) by f3(b,eps)=2*sqrt(b)*(b^2+1+2*sqrt(b))*eps, and Theorem 4.5 bounds ||A - Q~R~|| and ||I - Q~^T Q~|| by functions of (m,b,L,eps) only. This satisfies the ill-conditioned/rank-deficient robustness requirement of the QR checker.
claims.quote: Because it is performed on an orthonormal matrix, the growth factor in the upper triangular factor is bounded by 2, and we can bound the Frobenius norms of both computed factors by functions of the number of columns. Further, we can stably compute the T~ factor (needed to apply a blocked Householder update) from the upper triangular LU factor, a computationally cheaper method than using the Householder vectors themselves.

claims.claim: The output is exactly the LAPACK/ScaLAPACK compact-WY (Y unit-lower-triangular, T upper-triangular) representation — backward-compatible with existing libraries — which is precisely the flat geqrf-compatible (H, tau) form the contract requires; and the CHEAPER CholeskyQR-based shortcut (CholQR-HR / CholQR2-HR via LU(A-R)) is NOT safe for the contest's hard inputs because Cholesky fails once cond(A) > eps^{-1/2}, so the robust path must run Modified-LU on the orthonormal Q (TSQR-HR), not on A directly.
claims.quote: this basis-kernel representation is backward-compatible with (Sca)LAPACK and other libraries using the compact W Y representation... both CholeskyQR2 and CholQR2-HR cannot proceed to completion when the input matrix is ill-conditioned, i.e. cond(A) > eps^{-1/2}.

claims.claim: MAGMA's batched QR panel uses unblocked Householder (dgeqr2) with the standard LAPACK compact-WY block representation Q = I - V*T*V^T, NOT TSQR/CAQR — i.e. the production batched-QR baseline keeps the serial reflector-by-reflector dependency chain in the panel and does NOT use a communication-avoiding tree. This is negative evidence: no published MAGMA batched panel replaces the serial chain with O(log P) reduction.
claims.quote: The corresponding block of reflectors are applied to the trailing matrix using matrix-matrix (L3 BLAS) operations... The application of the block reflectors contains a preparatory stage (dlarft), during which a triangular factor T is computed from the V matrix and the scalars tau_i... such that Q = I - V x T x V^T.

claims.claim: The panel kernel assigns one thread per matrix row (>= m threads/block) and caches the m x nb panel in the register file; a hardware limit of 4 thread-blocks/SM means panels taller than 512 rows cause at least a 25% occupancy drop. This directly explains the user's grid-starved regimes (n=1024/2048/4096) and motivates a shared-memory panel kernel that decouples thread count from m (nb <= #threads <= m).
claims.quote: In a thread block, each thread possesses one row of the panel, so at least m threads are required for each thread block... we can schedule four thread blocks at maximum per SM, due to a hardware limitation. Panels taller than 512 would cause at least 25% drop in the thread occupancy per SM... We propose a second kernel that stores the panel in shared memory instead. This enables us use any number of threads to factorize the panel. The proposed kernel assumes nb <=#threads<= m.

claims.claim: The dlarft triangular-factor recurrence can be GEMM-ified: ALL the per-column dgemv calls aggregate into a single dgemm (T = V^T*V once, then a per-column triangular update T_{1:j-1,j} = -tau_j * T_{1:j-1,1:j-1} * T_{1:j-1,j}), leaving only the small triangular (dtrmv) work serial. This is the exact recurrence for making the compact-WY T cheap/tensor-core-friendly.
claims.quote: previous work [11] has shown that all the calls to dgemv can be aggregated into one dgemm call, while the dtrmv calls remain roughly unchanged... Algorithm 2: Improved dlarft  1  T_{1:nb,1:nb} = V^T_{1:n,1:n} x V_{1:n,1:n}  2 for j=1 to nb do  3  T_{1:j-1,j} = -tau_j T_{1:j-1,1:j-1} x T_{1:j-1,j}

claims.claim: Before panel fusion the panel kernels (dgeqr2) consumed 30-64% of batched-QR runtime (64.4% at 128x16 down to 30.3% at 256x256); kernel fusion cut this to 7-24%, after which the dgemm and the dlarft setup auxiliary kernels (dlacpy/dlaset) dominate. This quantitatively corroborates the user's 'panel is ~45% of runtime' bottleneck and shows fusion (not algorithm change) as the proven lever, while warning that the T-factor setup copies become the next bottleneck for tall-skinny sizes.
claims.quote: dgeqr2 kernels  64.4  55.09  45.86  30.28 ... [after fused geqr2] dgeqr2 kernels  24.37  11.37  10.26  7.81 ... the auxiliary kernels now contribute a noticeable amount of time, and even dominate the execution time for size 128 x 16. Recall that these auxiliary kernels are mostly called in a setup phase for computing the T factor

claims.claim: For dimensions that fit in registers/shared memory, a fully-fused fully-unrolled dgeqr2 using SERIAL reduction (not parallel tree reduction with syncs) for the column norm and v^T*A, with one warp factorizing multiple matrices, beats the best competition by up to 3.22x — and the published MAGMA panel uses NO tensor cores (the rank-updates are too narrow to saturate compute, and tensor-core use in MAGMA's own GEMM is left as future work).
claims.quote: it uses a serial reduction for computing the norm of a column, and for the v^T x A product.
